The White-bellied antbird Myrmeciza longipes exhibits distinct sexual dimorphism in adult body mass, with females typically reaching an ultimate wet weight of 23 grams [Wwi = 23 grams], while males are considerably heavier, attaining a maximum of 26.4 grams [Wwi = 26.4 grams]. This size disparity is consistent with the reversed sexual dimorphism observed across many thamnophilid species, though the degree of difference here is modest. Newly hatched chicks are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of just 3.7 grams [Wwb = 3.7 grams]. This initial mass represents a mere fraction of the adult female weight, underscoring the extreme altricial condition of the hatchlings, which require intensive brooding and nearly continuous provisioning by both parents during their early development in the understory nest.

Eggs incubated under controlled conditions at a mean temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] have a documented incubation period of 16 days [ab = 16 days], a value derived from studies of the closely related congener Oneillornis salvini. This duration is typical for a bird of this body mass and aligns well with the general incubation lengths reported for other medium-sized antbirds. The relatively short incubation period suggests a trade-off between developmental completeness at hatching and the heightened risk of nest predation that is characteristic of Neotropical forests. Following hatching, the altricial nestlings undergo a rapid phase of mass gain, fueled by a steady supply of arthropod prey delivered by both parents.

At the thermally stable conditions typical of an active, normothermic adult White-bellied antbird, which maintain a body temperature of approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the nestlings reach the critical developmental milestone of fledging after just 15 days [tx = 15 days]. This rapid achievement of first flight is an adaptation to the high predation pressure on nests, allowing the young to leave the vulnerable nest structure and begin exploring the dense understory vegetation. After fledging, the young birds remain dependent on their parents for several more weeks, learning to forage for insects and other small invertebrates while gradually improving their flight capabilities.

Sexual maturation in Myrmeciza longipes is a comparatively lengthy process given its small body size. Under the same active metabolic body temperature regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], males and females attain puberty, defined by the commencement of gonadal activity, at 45 days [tp = 45 days] after birth. This delayed maturation, relative to many other similarly sized passerines, may be linked to the species' complex social system and the need to acquire a high-quality territory in the saturated understory habitat. Basal metabolic rate for the White-bellied antbird was measured via flow-through respirometry on resting, post-absorptive individuals at their thermoneutral zone. The maximum recorded resting metabolic rate was 58.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 58.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value proportionally in line with expectations for a bird of its mass consuming a primarily insectivorous diet.
